reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) only discusses hot-cracking in laser cladding of a specific high-entropy alloy on steel due to thermal expansion mismatch, and the use of nickel-based interlayers to mitigate this. It does not provide evidence for the key premises regarding in-situ cooling, real-time feedback control, or the general efficacy of DED for repairing titanium alloys with hot-cracking sensitivity.
premises: In-situ substrate cooling and tailored alloying in DED can refine microstructure and minimize thermal gradients.
Real-time temperature monitoring and feedback control can keep the substrate below critical temperatures to prevent extended liquid-phase formation.
Reducing thermal gradients and liquid-phase duration will eliminate or significantly reduce hot-cracking.
The proposed DED process will produce a metallurgically fused repair with negligible hot cracking and superior mechanical properties compared to traditional fusion welding.
